source: Elements of Theology (Proclus, trans. Thomas M. Johnson, 1909; based on Thomas Taylor, 1816)

1.1: Every multitude partakes in some respect of The One.
1.2: For if it in no way or degree participates of The One, neither will the whole be one, nor each of the many things from which multitude arises, but each multitude will originate from certain or particular things, and this will continue ad infinitum.
1.3: And of these infinites each will be again infinite multitude.
1.4: For if multitude partakes in no respect of any one, neither as a whole nor through any of its parts, it will be in every respect indeterminate.
1.5: Each of the many, whichever you may assume, will be one or not one; and if not one will be either many or nothing.
1.6: But if each of the many is nothing, that likewise which arises from these will be nothing.
1.7: If each is many, each will consist of infinites without limit.
1.9: For there is no being constituted of infinites without limit, since there is nothing greater than the infinite itself; and that which consists of all is greater than each particular thing.
1.10: Neither is any thing composed of nothing.
1.11: Every multitude therefore partakes in some respect of The One.

2.1: Every thing which partakes of The One is alike one and not one.
2.2: For though it is not The One itself — since it participates of The One and is therefore other than it is — it experiences The One through participation, and is thus able to become one.
2.3: If therefore it is nothing besides The One, it is one alone, and will not participate of The One but will be The One itself.
2.4: But if it is something other than The One, it is alike one and non-one, — one being, since it partakes of oneness, but not oneness itself.
2.5: This therefore is neither The One itself, nor that which The One is.
2.6: And so far as it is multiplied it is not one; and so far as it experiences a privation of number or multitude it is one.
2.7: Every thing, therefore, which participates of The One is alike one and not one.

3.1: Every thing which becomes one, becomes so by the participation of The One, and is one so far as it experiences the participation of The One.
3.2: For if the things which are not one become one, they doubtless become so by a harmonious alliance and association with each other, and experience the presence of The One, though they are not that which The One is.
3.3: Hence they participate of The One, so far as they allow themselves to become one.
3.4: But if they are already one, they will not become one: for that which is, does not become that which it already is.
3.5: Every thing, therefore, which becomes one, becomes so by the participation of The One.

4.1: Every thing which is united is different from The One itself.
4.2: For if it is united it will participate in a certain respect of The One, so far as it is rightly said to be united.
4.3: That, however, which is a participant of The One is both one and not one.
4.4: But The One itself is not both one and not one.
4.5: For if The One is the same as the united, it will be infinite multitude.
4.6: And in a similar manner each of the things of which the united consists will be infinite multitude.
4.7: Every thing, therefore, which is united is different from The One itself.

5.1: All multitude is posterior to The One.
5.2: For if multitude is prior to The One, The One indeed will participate of multitude, but multitude which is prior will not participate of The One, since prior to the existence of The One that multitude was.
5.3: It is impossible that there should be a certain multitude which in no respect whatever participates of The One.
5.4: Multitude, therefore, is not prior to The One.
5.5: But if multitude and The One subsist simultaneously, neither is The One essentially many, nor is multitude The One, because they are directly opposite to each other by nature.
5.6: Hence multitude essentially will not be one, and this will be the case to infinity, which is impossible.
5.7: Multitude, therefore, according to its own nature participates of The One, and there is no thing of it which is not one.
5.8: Multitude will be wholly posterior to The One — participating indeed of The One, but not being participated by it.

6.1: Every multitude consists either of things united, or of unities.
6.2: It is evident that each of things many will not be itself multitude alone.
6.3: But if it is not multitude alone, it is either united or unities.
6.4: And if it partakes of The One it is united; but if it consists of things of which that which is primarily united consists, it will be unities.
6.5: For if The One itself exists, there is also that which primarily participates of it, and which is primarily united.
6.6: But this consists of unities: for if it consists of things united, again, things united consist of certain things, and this will be the case to infinity.
6.7: It is necessary, however, that what is primarily united should consist of unities.

7.1: Every thing productive of another is better than the nature of that which is produced.
7.2: For it is either superior, or inferior, or equal.
7.3: If unprolific, by reason of this fact it will be inferior to its producer.
7.4: But if it is productive of other things, it either produces that which is equal to itself and all beings will be equal to each other, or it produces that which is unequal to itself.
7.5: Hence it is not right that the thing produced should be equal to its producing cause.
7.6: Moreover, neither will that which produces ever be less than that which is produced by it.
7.7: The thing produced, therefore, is neither equal to nor better than its producing cause: and hence the producing cause is in every respect better than the nature of the thing produced.

8.1: That which is primarily good, and which is no other than The Good itself, is superior to all things which in any way whatever participate of good.
8.2: For if all beings desire good, it is evident that the Primary Good is beyond beings.
8.3: Hence that which is primarily good is nothing else than The Good itself.
8.4: The adding of any thing else to The Good is to diminish it by the addition, making it a certain or particular good instead of that which is simply good.

9.1: Every thing which is self-sufficient, either according to essence or energy, is better than that which is not self-sufficient, and depends on another cause for its perfection.
9.2: For if all beings naturally desire good, and one thing supplies well-being from itself, but another is indigent of something else, the one indeed will have the cause of good present, but the other separate and apart.
9.3: To the degree, therefore, that the former is nearer to that which supplies the object of desire, to that extent will it be superior to that which is indigent of a separate cause.

10.1: Every thing which is self-sufficient is inferior to that which is simply good.
10.2: For what else is the self-sufficient than that which from and in itself possesses good? But this is now full of good, and participates of it, but is not that which is simply good: for that is better than participation and plenitude, as has been demonstrated.
10.3: If therefore the self-sufficient fills itself with good, that from which it fills itself will be better than the self-sufficient.
10.4: And that which is simply good will not be indigent of any thing: for it does not desire any thing else, since the desiring would indicate a deficiency.
10.5: Nor is the simply good self-sufficient, for in that case it would be full of good, but not that which is primarily The Good.

11.1: All beings proceed from One First Cause.
11.2: For either there is no cause of any being, or the causes of all finite things revolve in a circle, or the ascent is to infinity.
11.3: If there is no cause of beings, there will be no order of things first and second, nor any science of beings.
11.4: But if causes revolve in a circle, the same things will be prior and posterior.
11.5: And if the addition of causes is to infinity, there will be no science of any being.
11.6: If, therefore, it is necessary that there should be a cause of beings, and there is not an ascent to infinity, there is a First Cause of beings, from which as from a root every thing proceeds.

12.1: The Principle and First Cause of all beings is The Good Itself.
12.2: For if all things proceed from one cause, it is necessary to call that cause either The Good, or that which is better than The Good.
12.3: But what can be greater than goodness? Since that which is better than other things is so called because it is a participant to a greater degree of the good.
12.4: If therefore The Good is that on which all beings depend, The Good is the Principle and First Cause of all things.

13.1: Every good has the power of uniting its participants, and every union is good; and The Good is the same as The One.
13.2: For if The Good is preservative of all beings, that indeed which is preservative and connective of the essence of every thing is The One.
13.3: For by The One all things are preserved, but dispersion expells every thing from its essence.
13.4: If this be the case, The Good will cause those things to which it is present to be one, and will connect and contain them through union.
13.5: Goodness therefore is union, and union is goodness, and The Good itself is one, and The One is that which is primarily Good.

14.1: Every being is either immovable or moved; and if moved, it is either moved by itself, or by another.
14.2: And if it is moved by itself it is self-motive, but if by another it is alter-motive.
14.3: Every nature, therefore, is either immovable, self-motive, or alter-motive.
14.4: For it is necessary, since there are alter-motive natures, that there also should be that which is immovable, and the self-motive nature as a medium between them.
14.5: For if every alter-motive thing is moved because it is moved by another, motions will be either in a circle, or they will proceed to infinity; but neither is possible.
14.6: Hence there will be something immovable, which first moves.
14.7: But if this be so, it is necessary that the self-motive exist, which unites alter-motive natures to that which is immovable, being a medium, moving and at the same time being moved.

15.1: Every thing which is able to return to itself is incorporeal.
15.2: For no body is, by reason of its nature, competent to return to itself.
15.3: For if that which is converted to anything is conjoined with that to which it is converted, all the parts of the body which is converted to itself will be conjoined with all the parts.
15.4: This however is impossible in body, and in all partible things.
15.5: For the whole of that which is partible is not conjoined with the whole, on account of the separation of its parts.
15.6: No body, therefore, is naturally able to return to itself.
15.7: Hence, if there is anything which has the power of returning to itself, it is incorporeal and impartible.

16.1: Every thing which is able to return to itself has an essence separate from every body.
16.2: For unless it was separate from every body whatsoever, it would not have a certain activity apart from body: since it is impossible that, the essence being inseparable from body, an activity proceeding from essence should be separate.
16.3: If any thing is inseparable in essence from body, it is similarly inseparable in activity.
16.4: But if this be so, it will not return to itself: for that which returns to itself has an activity separate from body.
16.5: Hence that which returns to itself is wholly separate from bodies.

17.1: Every thing which moves itself primarily, is able to return to itself.
17.2: For if it moves itself, and its motive energy is directed to itself, that which moves and that which is moved are at the same time one.
17.3: But if one part is that which moves, and another part is that which is moved, it will not be essentially self-motive.
17.4: If, however, one and the same thing moves and is moved, it will have the energy of moving to and within itself.
17.5: But it returns to that toward which it energizes.
17.6: Every thing, therefore, which primarily moves itself, is able to return to itself.

18.1: Every thing which imparts being to others is itself primarily that which it communicates to other natures.
18.2: For if it gives being, and makes the impartance from its own essence, that which it gives is subordinate to its own essence, which is truly greater and more perfect, since every nature which is able to constitute any thing is better than that which is constituted by it.
18.3: Hence the giver is essentially superior to that which is given, for the one exists primarily, but the other secondarily.

19.1: Every thing which is primarily inherent in a certain nature of beings is present to all the beings which are arranged according to that nature, conformably to one reason, and in the same manner.
19.2: For unless it was present to all of them in the same manner, but present to some and not to others, it would not be primarily in that nature, but in some things primarily, and in others secondarily.
19.3: For that which at one time exists, but at another time does not, does not exist primarily, nor of itself: but it is adventitious, and comes from some other place.

20.1: The essence of soul is beyond all bodies, the intellectual nature is beyond all souls, and The One is beyond all intellectual hypostases.
20.2: For every body is movable by another, but by the presence of soul it is moved of itself.
20.3: Soul is, however, by a much greater priority that which it imparts by its very being.
20.5: Again, soul which is moved from itself has an order secondary to the immovable nature.
20.6: But intellect moves, being immovable, and energizing always in the same manner.
20.7: Moreover, The One is prior to intellect.
20.8: For intellect, though it is immovable, yet is not The One; for it thinks itself, and energizes about itself.
20.9: The One, therefore, is beyond intellect, nor is there anything beyond The One: for The One and The Good are the same.

21.1: Every order, beginning from a monad, proceeds into a multitude co-ordinate to the monad, and the multitude of every order is referred to one monad.
21.2: For the monad, having the relation of a principle, generates a multitude allied to itself.
21.3: Hence one causal chain and one whole order has a decrement into multitude from the monad.
21.4: For there would no longer be an order, or a chain, if the monad remained of itself un-prolific.
21.5: But multitude is again referred to the one common cause of all coordinate natures.
21.6: In each order, therefore, there is one monad prior to the multitude, which imparts one ratio and connection to the natures arranged in it.

22.1: Every thing which subsists primarily and principally in each order is one, and is neither two, nor more than two, but is wholly one alone.
22.2: For, if it be possible, let there be two things which thus subsist.
22.3: But if it consists of each it will again be one, and there will not be two things which are first.
22.4: And if it be one of the two, each will not be first.
22.5: Nor, if both are equally primary, will each have a principal subsistence.
22.6: For that subsists primarily which is nothing else than that which it is said to be.
22.7: Both will not be first, but will be that of which both participating are thereby said to subsist primarily.

23.1: Every imparticipable produces the things which are participated: and all the natures which are participated strive for imparticipable essences.
23.2: For that which is imparticipable, having the relation of a monad, as subsisting from itself and not from another, and being exempt from participants, produces those things which may be participated.
23.3: For either it is of itself barren, remaining within itself, or it will impart something from itself.
23.4: But everything participating of another by which it is generated, is secondary to that which is similarly present to all things, and which fills all things from itself.
23.5: Hence if it is common to all things able to participate, it will be prior to all.
23.6: This is imparticipable, because it neither is nor can be participated by anything.

24.1: Every thing which participates is inferior to that which is participated by it; and that which is participated is inferior to that which is imparticipable.
24.2: For that which participates, since it is imperfect prior to participation, but becomes perfect through participation, is entirely secondary to that which is participated.
24.3: But that which is participated by a certain one and not by all, is on this account allotted an essence subordinate to that which is common to all things: for the latter is more allied to the cause of all.
24.4: The imparticipable, therefore, is the leader of things which are participated; but the latter are the leaders of participants.

25.1: Everything perfect proceeds to the generation of those things which it is able to produce, imitating the One Principle of all.
25.2: For as the one Principle by reason of its own goodness is unically constitutive of all beings, thus, also, those things which are posterior to the First Principle, on account of their perfection, hasten to generate beings inferior to their own essence: for perfection is a certain part or quality of The Good, and the perfect so far as it is perfect imitates The Good.
25.3: And that which is more perfect, the more perfect it is the more numerous are the progeny of which it is the cause.

26.1: Every cause which is productive of other things, itself abiding in itself, produces the natures posterior to itself, and those which are successive.
26.2: For if it imitates The One, but that immovably constitutes the things posterior to itself, everything which produces will possess in a similar manner the cause of productive energy.
26.4: For if through motion, the motion will be in it; and, being moved, it will no longer be The One, because it will be changed from The One.
26.5: Hence every producing cause produces subsequent natures from itself while abiding undiminished.

27.1: Every producing cause, by reason of its perfection and abundance of power, is productive of secondary natures.
27.2: For if it produced not on account of the perfect, but through a defect of power, it would not be able to preserve its own order immovable.
27.3: For that which imparts being to another thing through defect imparts subsistence to it through its own mutation and change in quality.
27.4: But every thing which produces remains such as it is, and in consequence of thus remaining that which is posterior to it proceeds into existence.
27.5: Hence, being full and perfect, it constitutes secondary natures immovably and without diminution.

28.1: Every producing cause constitutes things similar to itself, prior to such as are dissimilar.
28.2: For since that which produces is necessarily more excellent than the thing produced, they can never be simply the same with each other and equal in power.
28.3: But if they are not the same and equal, but different and unequal, they are either entirely separated from each other, or they are both united and separated.
28.4: If they are entirely separated, they will not accord with each other, and nowhere will that which proceeds from a cause sympathize with it.
28.5: But if it is more separated from than united to it, the thing generated will be more foreign than allied to that by which it is generated.
28.6: If, therefore, the things which proceed from causes have sympathy with them, things produced are in a greater degree allied to their producing causes than separated from them.
28.7: Every producing cause, therefore, constitutes things similar to itself prior to such as are dissimilar.

29.1: Every progression is effected through a similitude of secondary to primary natures.
29.2: For if that which produces constitutes similars prior to dissimilars, the similitude derived from the producing causes will constitute the things produced.
29.3: For similars are rendered similar through similitude, and not through dissimilitude.
29.4: If, therefore, progression in its diminution preserves a certain sameness of that which is generated with that which generates, it will have its nature through similitude.

30.1: Everything which is produced from a certain thing without a medium, abides in its producing cause, and proceeds from it.
30.2: For if every progression is effected while primary natures remain permanent, and is accomplished through similitude, that which is produced will in a certain respect abide in its producing cause.
30.3: For that which entirely proceeds will have nothing which is the same with the abiding cause.
30.4: But if it has anything in common with and united to it, it will abide in its cause in the same manner as that abides in itself.
30.5: So far, therefore, as that which is produced has something which is the same with the producing cause, it abides in it; but so far as it is different, it proceeds from it.
30.6: Being similar, it is at once both the same and different.
30.7: Hence it abides and at the same time proceeds, and does neither of these without the other.

31.1: Every thing which proceeds from another essentially, returns to that from which it proceeds.
31.2: For if it should proceed, indeed, but should not return to the cause of this progression, it would not desire its cause.
31.3: For everything which desires is converted to the object of its desire.
31.4: Moreover, every thing desires good, and to each thing the attainment of it is through the proximate cause.
31.5: Every thing, therefore, desires its cause: and the cause of being to any particular thing is likewise the cause of well-being to it.

32.1: Every conversion or return is effected through the similitude of the things converted to that to which they are converted.
32.2: For every thing which is converted hastens to be conjoined with its cause, and desires communion and colligation with it.
32.3: But similitude binds all things together, just as dissimilitude separates and disjoins all things.
32.4: If, therefore, conversion or return is a certain communion and contact, but all communion and all contact are through similitude, every conversion will be effected through similitude.

33.1: Every thing which proceeds from another and returns to it has a circular energy.
33.2: For if it returns to that from which it proceeds, it conjoins the end to the beginning, and the motion is one and continuous — emanating from the abiding cause and returning to it.
33.3: Hence all things proceed in a circle from causes to causes: but there are greater and less circles of conversions, some of which are to the natures immediately above the things which are converted, but others are to still higher natures, and so on to the Principle of all things.

34.1: Every thing which is converted according to nature makes its return to that from which it received the progression of its characteristic essence.
34.2: For if it is converted according to nature, it will have an essential desire for that to which it is converted.
34.3: Hence also it has a natural sympathy with it because it is cognate to its essence.
34.4: Either the being of each is the same, or the one is derived from the other.
34.5: It remains, therefore, that the one must derive its being from the other.
34.6: And if this be the case, the progression will be from that to which the conversion or return is according to nature.

35.1: Every thing caused abides in, proceeds from, and returns to, its cause.
35.2: For if it alone abided, it would in no respect differ from its cause, since it would be without separation and distinction from it.
35.3: For progression is accompanied with separation.
35.4: But if it alone proceeded, it would be unconjoined and deprived of sympathy with its cause.
35.5: And if it were alone converted, how can that which has not its essence from the cause be essentially converted to that which is foreign to its nature? Hence it follows that every thing must abide in its cause, proceed from, and return to it.

36.1: Of all things which are multiplied in progression the first are more perfect than the second, the second than those posterior to them, and after the same manner successively.
36.2: For if progressions separate productions from their causes, and there are diminutions of things secondary with respect to those which are first, it follows that first natures in proceeding are more conjoined with their causes.
36.3: But secondary natures are more remote from their causes.
36.4: Things, however, which are nearer and more allied to their causes are more perfect.
36.5: For causes are more perfect than things caused.

37.1: Of all things which subsist according to conversion, the first are more imperfect than the second, and the second than those that follow; but the last are the most perfect.
37.2: For if conversions are effected in a circle, and conversion or return is to that from which progression is derived, but progression is from that which is most perfect, hence conversion tends to the most perfect.
37.3: And if conversion first begins from that in which progression terminates, but progression terminates in that which is most imperfect, conversion will begin from the most imperfect.
37.4: Hence in things which subsist according to conversion, the most imperfect are the first, but the most perfect are the last.

38.1: Every thing which proceeds from many causes returns through as many, and every conversion is through the same causes which produced the progression.
38.2: For since both progression and return become through similitude, that which passes immediately from a certain thing likewise immediately returns to it.
38.3: But that which requires a medium in proceeding requires also a medium in returning.
38.4: Hence the return will be first to the medium, and then to that which is better than the medium.
38.5: Therefore the causes of being to each thing are equal in number to the causes of well-being.

39.1: Every being either alone essentially returns, or vitally, or gnostically.
39.2: For either it alone possesses being from its cause, or life with being, or it receives from thence a gnostic power.
39.3: So far, therefore, as every being alone is, it makes an essential conversion, but so far as it lives, a vital, and so far as it knows, a gnostic conversion.
39.4: For as it proceeded from its cause, so does it return to it.
39.5: The desire to return therefore is to some according to being alone; to others it is according to life, being a motion to more excellent natures; and to others it is according to knowledge, being a conscious perception of the goodness of their causes.

40.1: The natures which exist from and of themselves, and have a self-subsistent essence, precede those which proceed from another cause.
40.2: For if every nature which is self-sufficient is more excellent than that which depends on another cause; and that which produces itself is sufficient to itself with respect to essence; and that which is alone produced by another is not sufficient to itself — this being the case, the natures which are produced by themselves, and are self-subsistent, are more ancient than those which proceed into existence from another cause alone.

41.1: Every thing which is in another is alone produced by another; but every thing which is in itself is self-subsistent.
41.2: For that which is in another and is indigent of a subject can never be generative of itself.
41.3: For that which is naturally competent to generate itself does not require another base, because it is contained by itself, and is preserved in itself apart from a subject.
41.4: But that which abides, and is able to be established in itself, is productive of itself, itself proceeding into itself, and being connective of itself.

42.1: Every thing self-subsistent is able to return to itself.
42.2: For if it proceeds from itself, it will likewise return to itself.
42.3: For to that which is the source of a progression there is a return coordinate to the progression.
42.4: If it alone proceeded from itself, and did not return to itself, it would never strive for its characteristic good.
42.5: Every cause, however, is able to impart to that which proceeds from it both essence and well-being.
42.6: Hence that which is self-subsistent will impart this to itself, and hence it will return to itself.

43.1: Every thing which is able to return to itself is self-subsistent.
43.2: For if it returns to itself according to nature, it is perfect in the conversion to itself, and will possess essence from itself.
43.3: For from every thing to which there is a return according to nature, there is equally a progression according to essence.
43.4: If, therefore, it imparts well-being to itself, it will likewise undoubtedly impart being to itself, and will be the lord of its own nature.

44.1: Every thing which is able to return to itself through energy or activity, is likewise able to return to itself through essence.
44.2: For if it is capable of reverting to itself through its activity but not through its essence, it will be more excellent in activity than in essence.
44.3: For that which depends on itself is better than that which alone depends on another.
44.4: If, therefore, it is revertible to itself through the activity emanating from essence, it will also be allotted a revertible essence, so that it will not alone energize within itself but will depend on itself, and will be contained, connected, and perfected by itself.

45.2: For if it be generated, because of its generation it will be imperfect of itself, and will be indigent of perfection emanating from another.
45.3: Because, however, it produces itself, it is perfect and self-sufficient.
45.4: For every thing generated is perfected by another, which imparts generation to it not yet existing.
45.5: But if anything produces itself it is always perfect, since it is always present with the cause of itself.

46.2: For if it should be corrupted, it would depart from itself and would be without itself.
46.4: For, since it is one, it is at the same time cause and the thing caused.
46.5: But every thing which is corrupted, is corrupted departing from its cause.
46.6: But that which is self-subsistent never leaves its cause because it does not desert itself: for it is its own cause.
46.7: Every thing, therefore, which is self-subsistent is incorruptible.

47.1: Every thing self-subsistent is impartible and simple.
47.2: For if it is partible, since it is self-subsistent, it will constitute itself partible, and the whole will return to itself, and all will be in all itself.
47.4: Hence that which is self-subsistent is impartible.
47.6: For, if it is a composite, one thing in it will be less but another more excellent, and the more will be derived from the less excellent if the whole proceeds from itself.
47.7: Further, it would not be self-sufficient, since it would be indigent of its own elements.
47.8: Every thing, therefore, which is self-subsistent is impartible and simple.

48.1: Every thing which is not perpetual is either a composite or subsists in another.
48.2: For either it is dissoluble into those things of which it consists, and is entirely composed of the things into which it is dissolved, or it is indigent of a subject and, leaving the subject, it departs into nonentity.
48.3: But if it is simple in itself it will be indissoluble and incapable of being dissipated.

49.2: For there are two modes according to which it is necessary a thing should not be perpetual: the one arising from composition, and the other from a subsistence in something else as in a subject.
49.3: That which is self-subsistent, however, is neither a composite but a simple, nor in another but in itself.

50.1: Every thing which is measured by time, either according to essence or according to activity, is generation so far as it is measured by time.
50.2: For if it is measured by time it will belong to it to be, or to act, in time; and the was and the will be, which differ from each other, pertain to it.
50.3: If, therefore, the was and the will be are different, that which is measured by time is becoming to be and never is, but proceeds together with time.
50.4: It likewise does not stop in the same state of being, but is always receiving another and another being, just as the now in time is always another and another.
50.5: Hence it is not a simultaneous whole; for it subsists in a dispersion of temporal extension.
50.6: Generation, therefore, is such a kind of being.

51.1: Every thing self-subsistent is essentially exempt from the natures which are measured by time.
51.2: For if that which is self-subsistent is unbegotten, it will not be measured by time, according to existence.
51.3: For generation is conversant with the nature which is measured by time.
51.4: Hence nothing self-subsistent has its being in time.

52.1: Every thing eternal is a whole which subsists at once.
52.2: Whether it has its essence alone eternal, possessing the whole at once present, without having one of its parts already constituted and another to be constituted; or whether it has its activity as well as its essence at once present, it possessing this likewise collectively, abiding in the same measure of perfection, and as it were fixed immovably and without transition according to one and the same boundary.
52.3: For if the eternal, as the name denotes, is unceasing being, but being and becoming to be are different from unceasing being, it is not right that it should have one thing prior and another posterior.
52.4: For in that case it would be generation and not being.
52.5: But where there is neither prior nor posterior, nor was and will be, but being alone, and this a whole, there every thing subsists at once that which it is.

53.1: Eternity subsists prior to all eternal natures, and time exists prior to every thing which subsists in time.
53.2: For if everywhere the natures which are participated are prior to their participants, and imparticipables are prior to participated natures, it is evident that the eternal is one thing, the eternity which is in the eternal another, and eternity itself another.
53.3: And the first of these indeed subsists as a participant, the second as a thing participated, and the third as an imparticipable.
53.4: Eternity itself, likewise, is an eternity of eternities, and time itself is a time of times; and the one constitutes participated eternity, but the other participated time.

54.1: Every eternity is the measure of eternal natures, and every time is the measure of things in time; and these are the only two measures of life and motion in beings.
54.2: For every thing which measures, either measures according to a part, or it measures the whole at once when it is adapted to that which is measured.
54.3: That which measures, therefore, according to the whole is eternity, but that which measures according to parts is time.
54.4: Hence there are only two measures, the one of things eternal, but the other of things in time.

55.1: Every thing which subsists in time, either subsists through the whole of time, or has its hypostasis once in a part of time.
55.2: For if all progressions are through similitude, and things more similar to first natures subsist in union with them prior to those which are dissimilar, the medium between things which are at one time generated and those that exist always is that which is always becoming to be, conjoined indeed with the worse of the two through becoming to be, but through subsisting always imitating an eternal nature.

56.1: Every thing which is produced by secondary natures is produced in a greater degree by prior and more causal natures, by whom those which are secondary were also produced.
56.2: For if that which is secondary has the whole of its essence from that which is prior to it, its power of producing is also derived from thence.
56.3: But if it is allotted the power of producing from a superior cause, the things proceeding from it are effects through that which is prior to it.
56.4: Moreover, that it is likewise in a greater degree perfected from thence is evident.
56.5: For if that which is first imparts to that which is second the cause of producing, it will primarily possess this cause; and on this account that which is secondary generates, receiving from the first a secondary generative power.

57.1: Every cause energizes prior to the thing caused, and constitutes more effects posterior to it.
57.2: For so far as it is cause it is more perfect and more powerful than that which is posterior to it, and by reason of this is the cause of more effects.
57.3: For it is the province of a greater power to produce more, of an equal power to produce equal, and of a less power to produce a less number of effects.
57.4: Moreover, the effects which the thing caused is able to produce, the cause is in a greater degree able to produce.
57.5: All things, therefore, which the thing caused is naturally able to produce co-exist with and are produced by the cause.

58.1: Every thing which is produced by many is more composite than that which is produced by fewer causes.
58.2: For if every cause imparts something to that which proceeds from it, more causes will impart a greater number of gifts, but fewer causes a less number.
58.3: Hence, of participants some will consist of a greater number of things, but others of a less number.
58.4: Those, however, which proceed from a greater number of causes are more composite, but those from a less number of the same causes are more simple.

59.1: Every thing which is simple in essence is either better or worse than composite natures.
59.2: For if the beings which are the extremes of things are produced by fewer and more simple causes, but those which are in the middle by a great number of causes, the latter indeed will be composites, but of the former some are more simple according to that which is better, but others according to that which is worse.
59.3: Therefore the last of things, matter, is most simple, as well as the first of things, because it proceeds from the first alone.
59.4: But of these simplicities one is better than all composition, but the other according to that which is worse.

60.1: Every thing which is the cause of many effects is better than that which is allotted a power of producing few, and which produces the parts of those things the wholes of which the other constitutes.
60.2: For if the one is the cause of a few, but the other of many effects, but the former are parts of the latter, that which constitutes many effects will produce all that the other produces, but not vice versa.
60.3: Hence the former of these two is more powerful and more comprehensive.

61.1: Every thing which is more powerful is both more comprehensive in its productive energy, and in a more collected manner contains the things of which it is the cause.
61.2: For if it is the cause of a greater number of effects, but produces these all at once by reason of a more simple power, it will be more comprehensive.
61.3: But what is more comprehensive is more unical, and more collected in the causal reason.

62.1: Every simple cause is more excellent than any composite or co-ordinate cause.
62.2: For those which are composite, because they are constituted from many causes, are less powerful than such as are primary and simple, which generate more by a more simple productive energy.
62.3: That which is more comprehensive in productive energy is more powerful.
62.4: Hence the simple is more powerful and more excellent than the composite or co-ordinate cause.

63.1: All that which participates is inferior to the nature which it participates.
63.2: For that which participates, since it is imperfect prior to participation, but becomes perfect through participation, is entirely secondary to that which is participated; and through participation it acquires a certain good; and its good is from another.

64.1: Every thing participated is in the things which participate it, but the imparticipable is prior to all things.
64.2: For things participated subsist in the participants; but that which is imparticipable is not in any thing, but all things which are participable subsist from it as from a cause.
64.3: Hence that which is participated is in participants; but the imparticipable is exempt from all things, and prior to that which is participated.

65.1: Every thing which is participable proceeds from the imparticipable, and is present to a certain participant alone.
65.2: For since it is present to a participant, it is in that thing to which it is present; and it imparts itself to one thing, but is not common to all.
65.3: But the imparticipable is common to all things which are able to participate of it, and is equally present to all, not being in any thing, but being the cause of that which is in the participant.
65.4: Hence the participated proceeds from the imparticipable, as the particular from the universal cause.

66.1: Every thing which is participated, as being in a participant, is made finite by the participant.
66.2: For if it is in another, it is defined and determined by that in which it subsists, since every thing which is in another is bounded by that other.
66.3: The participant, therefore, bounds that which is participated; and that which is participated, by being in a participant, participates of bound; so that the imparticipable alone is exempt from all bound which comes from participants.

67.1: Every productive cause produces things similar to itself prior to things dissimilar, and establishes prior to all others those things which are in the highest degree allied and similar to itself.
67.2: For since every productive cause produces by its very being, and as it is, the things produced which are more perfectly allied to it are more similar to it.
67.3: Hence the most similar are produced first, but the least similar later; so that the similars are prior to the dissimilars.

68.1: Every thing which proceeds from any cause, and is established in it, is either coordinate with it in genus, or is analogous to it, or possesses the same peculiarity with it in a lesser degree.
68.2: For if the productive cause constitutes things similar prior to things dissimilar, the things which proceed from it will not be entirely dissimilar to the productive cause; but they will be partly similar, and partly dissimilar, so that each either participates of the same genus, or is analogous to it, or possesses a lesser power of the same peculiarity.

69.1: Every thing which participates of any power or essence participates of it either wholly, or according to a part.
69.2: For that which is participated is either perfectly imparted, or is imparted in part.
69.3: If wholly, and the thing which participates is not one with the participated, either the participated will not be participated without being divided among its participants, and will thus be divided and lessened; or it will be in many participants at one and the same time.
69.4: But if it is imparted in part, the participant will receive a part of the participated, and not the whole.

70.1: Every thing which participates of The One participates of it either as a whole or according to a part.
70.2: For if it is participated, it is either participated as a whole by the participant, and thus The One will be in the participant, and there will be as many ones as there are participants; or it is participated according to a part.
70.4: If therefore it is participated as a whole by all, all things will be one; or it is participated as a whole by one alone, and not by all.
70.5: But if it is participated according to a part, The One will be divided.
70.6: Hence how it is that things participate of The One, though it is impartible, is a problem requiring a profound speculation.

71.1: Every thing which is participated, being wholly in its participants, is either divided among them, or is whole in each.
71.2: For if it is whole in each, it is present to each as a whole, and the same thing is wholly in many: which is possible in incorporeals.
71.3: For an incorporeal is not excluded from another, since there is no interval to prevent it.
71.4: But if it is divided among them, being divided it is diminished in each of the things in which it is present.
71.5: That which is incorporeal and impartible, however, can be whole in each without diminution: and hence it is participated as a whole by each of the participants.

72.1: All things are in all, but in each appropriately.
72.2: For in intellect all things are intellectually; but in soul all things are in a psychical manner; and in nature all things exist naturally.
72.3: And in each thing all the others are present according to the power of each recipient; for all things are in all according to the appropriate capacity of each.

73.1: Every thing which is able to know itself is able to know both intellectual natures and the cause of all, viz.
73.3: For if it knows itself, and returns to itself, it participates of intellect, since intellect is that which gives knowledge to all things which know.
73.4: And if it participates of intellect, it is able to know intellectual essences, since these are kindred to intellect.
73.5: And if it knows intellectual essences, it is able to know the cause of all, viz.
73.6: The Good, since this is the principle of intellectual essences.

74.1: Every thing which knows itself possesses in itself a sufficient principle of knowing all things.
74.2: For if it knows its own essence, and its essence is united to all things — for it subsists from the First, and is itself the cause of secondary natures — it will in knowing itself know these likewise, being itself the principle of their knowledge.

75.2: For it both proceeds from and returns to itself.
75.3: And if it returns to itself, and is converted to itself as to its own proper essence, it will possess a self-knowledge.
75.4: For in every thing which is converted the converging and that to which the conversion is are the same.
75.5: That which is self-subsistent, therefore, is self-knowing; and that which is primarily self-subsistent is primarily self-knowing.

76.1: Every thing which knows itself is in itself, and the energy of it terminates in itself.
76.2: For if the knowing and the known are the same — since it knows itself — and the energy of knowledge is directed to the known, the energy of that which knows itself terminates in itself.
76.3: And if the energy of it terminates in itself, and it is present to itself through its energy, it is in itself, and its subsistence is in itself; i.e., it is self-subsistent.

77.1: Every thing which is produced by another, and is moved by another, knows by another; but that which moves and is moved by itself, and produces and is produced by itself, knows by itself and knows itself.
77.2: For the principle of motion and action in any being is analogous to the principle of knowledge in it.
77.3: Since therefore that which moves itself has its principle of motion within itself, it has likewise the principle of knowledge within itself, and by this knows itself.

78.1: Every thing which knows by another knows things which differ from itself.
78.2: For if it knows by another, the principle of its knowledge is in another, and it knows through that other.
78.3: But if this be so, it knows according to the other, and not according to itself.
78.4: Hence it knows things foreign to itself, and the objects of its knowledge are other things, and not itself.

79.1: Every thing which is productive of other things knows the things which it produces.
79.2: For the productive cause does not produce blindly and without intelligence, but according to knowledge: for it constitutes by its very being, and its being is intellectual.
79.3: Moreover, intellectual natures produce by their very being and by their intelligence, since in them being and intellect are the same.
79.4: Hence the productive cause knows the things which it produces.

80.1: Every intellect thinks all things together and non-discursively.
80.2: For its thought is not extended in time, but is one and stable and the same; and it thinks all things at once.
80.3: For if it thinks successively, its thought will be in time; and it will not think all at once, but will pass through its objects one by one, which is the mode of discursive reason; and it will not possess all the objects of its thought at once, but will have some things present and others to come.

81.1: Every intellect is indivisible and without parts.
81.2: For if it is incorporeal and immovable, it is not divisible, since divisibility and extension are characteristics of corporeal things.
81.3: And if it is indivisible, it is without parts.
81.4: Hence intellect is one and a whole, and is not divided into parts.
81.5: For that which thinks all things together is indivisible; since that which is divided into parts does not think all things together, but each part thinks certain things, and the whole thinks collectively by means of the parts.

82.2: For if it always thinks, and its thinking is the same as its being — since in intellect being and thinking are identical — it is always intellect.
82.3: For it will not be at one time intellect and at another time not, since its being is unchanging.

83.2: For if it thinks all things together, and its thought is not according to time, but is all at once present, then its thinking is not a motion or transition, but a stable and eternal knowledge of itself and of all things.

84.1: Every intellect has its hypostasis from The Good, and tends to The Good.
84.2: For every thing tends to that from which it proceeds.
84.3: And if it proceeds from The Good, it tends to The Good.
84.4: But it proceeds from The Good: for the First is The Good, and the productive power of the First extends to all things, producing each in its proper order and nature.
84.5: Hence intellect, which is the first of beings after The Good, proceeds directly from The Good, and tends to The Good as to its cause.

85.1: Every intellect is a God, but not every God is an intellect.
85.2: For if the Gods are more than intellects, and intellects are a multitude proceeding from one intellect, intellect is not The Good itself, but subsists after The Good.
85.4: Hence every God transcends intellect; but intellect, being deified, is a God by participation.

86.1: Every nature which is truly being is infinite, neither through multitude nor through magnitude, but through the power of itself.
86.2: For if it is truly being, and always is, and is not measured by time, its being is not finite, and not bounded by time.
86.3: But if its power is not finite according to time, and it is truly being, it is infinite in power.
86.4: For that which has infinite power is truly being, since it has an inexhaustible power of subsistence.

87.1: Every eternal nature is being, but not every being is eternal.
87.2: For if the eternal always is, it participates of being: but that which always participates of being, and has an always co-subsistent with its being, is eternal.
87.3: The being, however, which is in time is not eternal: for it is measured by time, and the always of it proceeds according to prior and posterior.
87.4: Hence not every being is eternal, though every eternal nature is being.

88.1: Every nature which is truly being is either prior to eternity, or in eternity, or participates of eternity.
88.2: For if it is truly being, it either is eternity itself, or is measured by eternity, or participates of eternity through that which is measured by eternity.
88.3: The first of these is prior to eternity; the second is eternal itself; and the third participates of eternity.
88.4: But all of them are truly being.

89.1: Every nature which is truly being consists of bound and infinity.
89.2: For since it is a whole, it participates of bound, which collects multitude into whole.
89.3: And since it has an inexhaustible power, it participates of infinity.
89.4: For that which is unbounded in power is in a certain sense infinite.
89.5: Hence every nature which is truly being consists of bound and infinity, being a mixture of the two primary genera.

90.1: The first bound and the first infinity subsist by themselves, prior to every thing which is mixed from them.
90.2: For if bound and infinity are mixed in beings, each must subsist by itself prior to the mixture: for that which exists in another proceeds from that which exists by itself.
90.3: Hence there is a bound which subsists by itself prior to all things which are bounded, and an infinity which subsists by itself prior to all things which participate of infinity.

91.1: Every power which is finite according to multitude is likewise finite according to the magnitude of its energy.
91.2: For if the energy proceeds according to the power, it will be limited in the same manner as the power is limited.
91.3: And if the power is finite according to multitude, the energy will likewise be finite.
91.4: Hence every finite power has a finite energy.

92.1: Every multitude of infinite powers depends on one first infinity, which is not a participated power, nor does it subsist in things which are endued with power, but by and of itself.
92.2: For all participated infinities proceed from the imparticipable infinity.
92.3: But if the first infinity is infinite, its power is not finite; since that which is finite in power will not be able to be the principle of all infinite powers.
92.4: Hence the first infinity is itself infinite in power, and is the cause of all infinite things.

93.1: Every infinite which is in true beings is neither infinite to superior natures, nor is it infinite in a simple manner.
93.2: For that which is above it is its principle, and bounds and defines it: since it proceeds from the imparticipable infinity through the participated.
93.3: But to things subordinate and more partial it is infinite, since they are unable to comprehend its power.
93.4: Hence it is infinite to things inferior, but not to things superior.

94.1: Every perpetuity is indeed a certain infinity, but not every infinity is a perpetuity.
94.2: For the perpetual is infinite according to time: for it is always, and has an inexhaustible power of being in time.
94.3: But the infinite in power is not on this account perpetual: for that which is beyond time, if it had an inexhaustible power, would not for this reason be perpetual, since the perpetual is that which always exists in time.

95.1: Every power which is more simple is more infinite than that which is multiplied.
95.2: For that which is simpler is nearer to the First, and more proximate to infinity itself, from which all powers participate of infinity.
95.3: Hence the simpler is in a greater degree infinite, and has a more inexhaustible power.

96.1: Every thing which is more powerful can act on a greater number of things and extend its activity farther.
96.2: For if one power is greater than another, it constitutes more effects, and produces through a wider range of influence.
96.3: Hence the more powerful a being is, the greater is the extent of its productive activity.

97.1: Every archical cause in each series or causal chain imparts to the whole series its characteristic; and that which the cause is primarily, the series is according to diminution.
97.2: For the monad imparts its own peculiarity to the things which are arranged under it, and these possess the same characteristic which the monad primarily has, but in a lesser degree.
97.3: Hence each order is denominated from its monad, and the monad is the cause of the characteristic of the whole order.

98.1: Every separate cause is at one and the same time everywhere and nowhere.
98.2: For if it is everywhere, being present to all things, it is not nowhere.
98.3: But if it is separate and exempt, it is not in any thing in which it is present, but is prior to all.
98.4: Hence it is at the same time everywhere, through its productive power, and nowhere, through its exemption from all things.

99.1: Every cause which is productive through essence produces effects similar to itself, but the cause which produces through participation generates things dissimilar in a greater degree.
99.2: For the productive cause which acts through its very essence produces what it is by its very being.
99.3: But that which produces through participation acts not by its very essence but by what it has received from another.
99.4: Hence the latter imparts to its effects something more foreign to itself, and the effects are less similar to it than to the primary cause from which the participant received its power.

100.1: Every series is established under one cause which is its proper monad, and the whole series is unified by this monad.
100.2: For if each order begins from a monad, as has been demonstrated, and the multitude of the order is referred to one monad, the whole series subsists in a unified manner by reason of its monad, and is one order through the unific power of the monad which governs it.

101.1: Every divine being is both imparticipable and participated, but The One which is First is imparticipable alone.
101.2: For since every participated being subsists in a participant, and the imparticipable is prior to that which is participated, and there is a certain nature which is imparticipable alone, viz.
101.3: The One — for if The One were participated, it would be in a participant, and would not be simply The One — hence The One is imparticipable alone.
101.4: But the things which come after The One, though they are imparticipable according to their own proper hypostasis, are yet participated through that which proceeds from them and subsists in participants.

102.1: All divine unities are superessential, and all divine essences are united.
102.2: For if the divine unities are the flowers and summits of beings, they transcend the order of essence, being the causes of essence.
102.3: But all divine essences are united through their participation of the divine unities which illuminate them.
102.4: Hence the divine unities are superessential, and the divine essences are united.

103.1: Every divine unity is whole and complete in itself.
103.2: For if it is one, and the one is impartible, it is a whole without parts and complete without diminution.
103.3: But if it is complete without diminution and a whole, it has all its power in itself, and neither is indigent of another for its perfection, nor imparts any part of itself to that which participates of it, but remains complete while that which participates of it likewise receives completeness from it.

104.1: Every henad or divine unity is both ineffable and unknown.
104.2: For if it is superessential, it transcends all essence and all knowledge.
104.3: For knowledge is of essence and is united to essence.
104.4: But that which is superessential transcends knowledge.
104.5: Hence the divine unity is ineffable and unknown; and from the participants of the divine unities we denominate the unities themselves, knowing them from their effects.

105.1: Every God is self-perfect and the cause of perfection to the things which participate of him.
105.2: For if all things desire The Good, and God is more allied to The Good than all other beings, he will be self-perfect, not requiring the perfection of another, but being full of The Good itself.
105.3: And being self-perfect, he imparts perfection to the things which participate of him, giving to each that perfection which it is adapted to receive.

106.1: Every God is a measure of all beings.
106.2: For if God is more proximate to The One than other beings, and The One is the measure of all, God will be a measure to those things which proceed from him.
106.3: For every monad is the measure of the things which are co-ordinate with it: since the monad is the principle of number, and number is the measure of all things.

107.1: Every God, being participated by beings, imparts to them his own characteristic from himself.
107.2: For since the things which participate of the Gods are ranked according to the Gods, and each receives the peculiarity of that God from which it is produced, every God imparts his peculiarity to the things that participate of him.
107.3: For the monad imparts the characteristic of the order to all the things which are co-ordinate with it.

108.1: Every God is prior to good as its principle, and is beyond good; but not so as to be inferior to good.
108.2: For The Good is the first principle of all things, and God proceeds from The Good as being conjoined with The One; for The Good and The One are the same.
108.3: Hence God is immediately after The One, and is more proximate to it than good as good.
108.4: For God participates of The One as a unity, and is elevated above the level of essence and good, being superessential.

109.1: Every God is an imparticipable unity from which the participated unities proceed.
109.2: For if the Gods are unities, and the imparticipable is prior to the participated, there must be unities which are imparticipable, from which the participated unities derive their subsistence.
109.3: But these imparticipable unities are the Gods themselves, who are the principles of all the participated and participable unities.

110.1: Every God illuminates with his own light all the things which are able to participate of him, extending his goodness even to the most distant things.
110.2: For since the Gods are productive of good, and every thing which is productive of good imparts it to secondary natures, the Gods illuminate all things with their divine light.
110.3: Nor is any thing so remote from them that it does not receive some illumination from them; for the power of the Gods is not finite, but extends to all things.

111.1: Every God who is participated by all things is participated according to the capacity of each participant.
111.2: For since all things desire The Good, and the Gods are most proximate to The Good, all things desire to participate of the Gods.
111.3: But all things participate of the Gods according to their own capacity: for the participation is measured by the capacity of the participant, not by the power of that which is participated.

112.1: Every God by his very being benefits all things.
112.2: For since the Gods are most proximate to The Good, they are most beneficent.
112.3: And since they are most beneficent, they benefit all things by their very being, and not through deliberate choice alone, since their being is identical with their goodness.

113.2: For if God is beyond essence and time — being more proximate to The One than essence is, and prior to time — he is eternal.
113.3: For that which is beyond time is either prior to eternity, or in eternity, or the same with eternity.
113.4: But the Gods are prior to eternity and intellect, and hence are eternal in a more primary manner than intellect and beings.

114.1: Every God is self-perfect and abundantly productive.
114.2: For if the Gods are full of The Good, and that which is full of The Good is self-perfect, the Gods are self-perfect.
114.3: And since every thing which is perfect proceeds to the generation of secondary natures, and is productive of things posterior to itself, the Gods, being self-perfect in the highest degree, are in the highest degree productive of things posterior to themselves.

115.1: Every God is participable, and yet no one of the Gods is participable by all beings alike.
115.2: For if there are many Gods, each has his own peculiarity, and each is participated according to his peculiar characteristic.
115.3: But if each is participated according to his peculiarity, not all things can participate of each equally: for the peculiarity of each God is adapted to certain participants more than to others.
115.4: Hence every God is participable, yet not by all beings alike, but by those which are adapted to his peculiar power and characteristic.

116.1: Every God, being participated by secondary natures, remains whole and undiminished.
116.2: For since the Gods are impartible unities, and that which is impartible is not diminished by being participated, the Gods remain whole and undiminished while being participated.
116.3: For the participant does not receive a part of the God, but participates of the God according to the measure of its own capacity; and the God remains entire and undiminished, even though participated by many.

117.1: Every God is beyond all intellect, and beyond all soul.
117.2: For since the Gods are unities, and intellect is a multitude — for intellect thinks itself and knows beings, which is a certain kind of multitude — the Gods, as pure unities, are beyond intellect.
117.3: And since soul is self-motive, and motion is a certain kind of plurality, the Gods, being beyond plurality, are beyond soul.

118.1: Every God who is more universal produces his own specific effects through gods that are more partial.
118.2: For the more universal Gods constitute all things through those which are more partial, just as The Good, being universal cause, constitutes all things through the subordinate principles.
118.3: Hence the divine progressions descend from the most universal to the most particular, and from the most simple to the most composite.

119.1: Every God has an arrangement either as a monad or as a multitude co-ordinate to a monad, or as being in a monad.
119.2: For either the God is himself a monad and the principle of a series, or he is co-ordinate with others in a series, or he is a member of a series under a monad.
119.3: These three arrangements exhaust the possible positions of any God in relation to the divine order.

120.1: Every God has a triple power, of abiding, of proceeding, and of reverting.
120.2: For as every being abides in its cause, proceeds from it, and reverts to it, so every God abides in The One, proceeds from The One, and reverts to The One.
120.3: And this triple power belongs to every God, as to every being.

121.1: Every thing divine has a goodness which exceeds the ordinary goodness of beings.
121.2: For since the Gods are more proximate to The Good than all other beings, and since The Good is the cause of all good, the Gods participate of The Good in a more eminent manner than other beings.
121.3: Hence every thing divine has an extraordinary and transcendent goodness.

122.1: Every divine intellect is uniform and perfect.
122.2: For if it is divine, it is deified, and being deified, it is united to the Gods, and partakes of their unity.
122.4: And if it is uniform, it is perfect: for that which is united to the Gods is filled with their perfection.

123.1: Every God is prior to intellect and prior to being.
123.2: For being is the first of the participable natures, as has been demonstrated.
123.3: But the Gods, as pure unities, are beyond participation, and hence prior to being.
123.4: And intellect, being a participated essence, is likewise posterior to the Gods.
123.5: Hence every God is prior to intellect and prior to being.

124.1: Every participant of the divine unity is deified, and every deified being participates of a divine unity.
124.2: For if the Gods are unities, and the things which participate of the Gods participate of their unities, the things which participate of the Gods are deified through participating of divine unities.
124.3: Conversely, every deified being is so through participating of a divine unity, since the Gods are unities.

125.1: Every God both remains in himself and proceeds to all things.
125.2: For if the Gods are self-sufficient and complete, they remain in themselves.
125.3: And if they are productive of all things through their power, they proceed to all things.
125.4: But this procession does not diminish their abiding: for it is not a motion in place, but an illumination which, proceeding from the Gods, is present to all things which are able to receive it, while the Gods themselves remain in their own proper hypostasis.

126.1: All things are either in The One, or are from The One.
126.2: For since all things proceed from The One, and are constituted by The One, all things are in The One as in their cause, and are from The One as from their principle.
126.3: And all things tend to The One as to their end, desiring that unity which they have lost through their progression into multitude.

127.1: Every thing which is in any way whatever a cause of something divine is itself more divine than that of which it is the cause.
127.2: For if the cause is more excellent than the thing caused, as has been demonstrated, then among divine things the cause is more divine.
127.3: Hence that which is the cause of any divine thing is more divine than that divine thing of which it is the cause.

128.1: Every thing which is more divine is more uniform than that which is less divine.
128.2: For the divine is characterized by unity, as has been demonstrated.
128.3: Hence that which is more divine participates more of unity, and is therefore more uniform.
128.4: And that which is less divine is more multiplied and less uniform.

129.1: All the divine orders are constituted according to the number of their principles and monads.
129.2: For since every order proceeds from a monad and tends to a monad, the number of the orders corresponds to the number of the monads.
129.3: And since the divine orders are characterized by their monads, the divine orders are constituted according to the number of the divine monads.

130.1: All things are distributed into three orders: those that are causes, those that are constituted by causes, and those that are media between causes and effects.
130.2: For in every procession there is a first which is the cause, a last which is the effect, and a medium which partakes of both.
130.3: The medium is produced by the first, but is itself productive of the last; and it converts the last toward the first.
130.4: Hence all things are in one of these three orders.

131.1: Every divine progression is from a more universal to a more partial existence.
131.2: For the Gods produce from themselves natures more partial than themselves.
131.3: The most universal God produces the most universal effects; the more particular Gods produce more particular effects.
131.4: Hence the divine progressions advance from the universal to the particular, from unity to multitude, and from simplicity to composition.

132.1: All divine orders are comprehended within each other, the more universal comprehending the more particular.
132.2: For since the more universal is the cause of the more particular, the more universal comprehends the more particular in itself as in its cause.
132.3: Hence the highest divine order comprehends all the lower orders in itself; and each lower order comprehends all orders still lower.

133.1: Every thing which produces another without being diminished or changed, does so by abundance of power.
133.2: For if it remains what it is, and yet gives rise to another thing, it gives by abundance and not by diminution.
133.3: Hence the producing cause produces by its very fullness and abundance, not by losing anything of itself.
133.4: And this is the characteristic of the divine production: it produces by abundance, not by division.

134.1: Every divine body participates of soul, and every divine soul participates of intellect, and every divine intellect participates of a unity.
134.2: For if the Gods deify all the things which participate of them, and if bodies, souls, and intellects can participate of the Gods, then divine bodies participate of soul, divine souls of intellect, and divine intellects of the divine unity.
134.3: In this way all the divine orders are connected to the Gods.

135.1: Every divine intellect is participated by souls which it perfects.
135.2: For since intellect is above soul, and soul participates of what is above itself, divine souls participate of divine intellect.
135.3: And since intellect perfects those natures which participate of it, the divine intellect perfects the souls which participate of it.

136.1: Every God who is more universal and ranks nearer to the First, is participated by a more universal genus of beings; but the God who is more partial and more remote from the First, is participated by a more partial genus of beings.
136.2: And as being is related to being, so is unity to divine unity.
136.3: For if there are as many beings as there are unities, and vice versa, and one unity is participated by one being, it is evident that the order of beings proceeds according to the order of the unities, being assimilated to the order prior to beings: and more universal beings are connascent with more universal unities, but more partial beings with more partial unities.

137.1: Every unity with the one constitutes the being which participates of it.
137.2: For The One, since it constitutes all things, so likewise it is the cause of the unities which are participated, and of the beings which depend on these unities.
137.3: But the unity of every being produces the peculiarity which shines forth in that particular being.
137.4: And The One indeed is the cause of being simply; but unity is the cause of alliance, because it is connascent with The One.

138.1: Of all the deified natures which participate of the divine peculiarity, the first and highest is Being itself.
138.2: For if being is beyond intellect and life, as has been demonstrated, and if it is likewise after The One the cause of the greatest number of effects, being will be the highest deified nature.
138.3: For it is more unical than life and intellect, and is on this account entirely more venerable.
138.4: But there is no other prior to it except The One.

139.1: All things which participate of the divine unities begin from being, but end in a corporeal nature.
139.2: For being is the first of participants, but body the last: for we say that there are divine bodies.
139.3: For the highest of all the genera of bodies, souls, and intellects are attributed to the Gods, so that in every order things analogous to the Gods may connect and preserve secondary natures.
139.4: The divine genus, therefore, subsists corporeally, psychically, and intellectually: and it is evident that all these are divine according to participation.

140.1: All the powers of divine natures, having a supernal origin, and proceeding through appropriate media, extend even to the last of things and to the terrestrial regions.
140.2: For neither does any thing intercept these powers, and exclude their presence from all things.
140.3: For they are not in want of places and intervals, on account of their unrestrained transcendency with respect to all things, and a presence every where unmingled.
140.4: When therefore conformably to a concurrence of many causes, an aptitude to the participation of the Gods is ingenerated in some nature, then a certain divinity is unfolded into light, always possessing his appropriate allotment, and always extending the participation of himself, similarly to illuminations from the sun.

141.1: Every providence of the Gods is twofold, one exempt from the natures for which it provides, but the other co-ordinated with them.
141.2: For some divine essences, through their hyparxis and the peculiarity of their order, are entirely expanded above the illuminated natures.
141.3: But others, which are of the same order, provide for things subordinate of the same co-ordination; these likewise imitating the providential activity of the exempt Gods, and desiring to fill secondary natures with the good which they are able to impart.

142.1: The Gods are present to all things in the same manner, but all things are not in the same manner present to the Gods; but every thing participates of their presence according to its own order and power.
142.2: For it is necessary that the different participation of the same things should become different either from the participant, or from that which is participated.
142.3: But every divine nature always has the same order, and is free from any relation to all things, and is unmixed.
142.4: It follows therefore that the mutation must arise and subsist from the participants, and that at different times they are differently present to the Gods.

143.1: All inferior natures yield to the presence of the Gods, though the participant may be adapted to participation.
143.2: Every thing alien recedes from the divine light, but all things are illuminated at once by the Gods.
143.3: For divine natures are always more comprehensive and more powerful than the things which proceed from them.
143.4: But the inaptitude of the participants is the cause of the deprivation of divine illumination: for this inaptitude obscures it by its own imbecility.

144.1: All beings, and all the distributions of beings, extend as far in their progressions as the orders of the Gods.
144.2: For the Gods produce beings with themselves, nor is it possible for any thing to subsist, and to receive measure and order external to the Gods; for all things are perfected, disposed, and measured by the power of the Gods.
144.3: Prior therefore to the last genera in beings the Gods preexist, who likewise adorn these genera, and impart to them life, form and perfection, and convert them to The Good.

145.1: The peculiarity of every divine order pervades through all secondary natures, and imparts itself to all the subordinate genera of beings.
145.2: For if beings proceed as far as the orders of the Gods extend, in every genus of beings there is a supernally-illuminated peculiarity of the divine powers.
145.3: For every thing receives from its proximate appropriate cause the peculiarity according to which that cause is allotted its hypostasis.
145.4: And there is the same mode of reasoning with respect to the peculiarities of the other divine powers.
145.5: For all things depend on the Gods.
145.6: Truly, all things are full of Gods.

146.1: The ends of all the divine progressions are assimilated to their principles, preserving a circle without a beginning and without an end, through the return of all to their principles.
146.2: For if every thing which has proceeded returns to its own principle from which it proceeded, much more will universal orders having proceeded from their summit again return to it.
146.3: But the return of the end to the beginning renders the whole order one, definite, and tending to itself, and exhibiting through this tendency the uniform which is in the multitude.

147.1: The summits of all the divine orders are assimilated to the ends of the natures which are proximately above them.
147.2: For if it is necessary that there should be a continuity of the divine progression, and that each order should be bound together by appropriate media, it is necessary that the summits of secondary should be conjoined with the ends of primary orders.
147.3: But this contact becomes through similitude.
147.4: Hence there will be a similitude of the principles of an inferior to the ends of a proximately superior order.

148.1: Every divine order is united to itself in a threefold manner, viz. by the summit which is in it, by its middle, and by its end.
148.2: For the summit having a power which is most unical transmits union to all the causal chain, and unites the whole of it, supernally abiding in itself.
148.3: But the middle, extending to both extremes, binds together the whole order about itself; transmitting indeed the gifts of primary divine natures, but extending the powers of those which are last and inserting communion in all of them.
