148.4: And the end again returning to the beginning, and recalling the proceeding powers, imparts similitude and convergency to the whole order.

149.1: Every multitude of the divine unities is bounded by number.
149.2: For if it is most proximate to The One it will not be infinite: for the infinite is not connascent with The One, but alien to it.
149.3: Indeed, if multitude of itself or essentially departs from The One, it is evident that infinite multitude is perfectly destitute of it.
149.4: The multitude of the Gods therefore is not infinite.
149.5: Hence it is uniform and finite, and is more finite than every other multitude: for it is nearer to The One than all other multitude.

150.1: Every nature which proceeds in the divine orders is not naturally adapted to receive all the powers of its producing cause.
150.2: Nor in brief are secondary natures able to receive all the powers of the natures prior to themselves, but these have certain powers exempt from things in an inferior order, and incomprehensible by the beings posterior to themselves.
150.3: For if the peculiarities or characteristics of the Gods differ from each other, those of the subordinate preexist in the superior divinities; but those of the superior, since they are more universal, are not in the subordinate.

151.1: Every paternal order or genus in the Gods is primary, and pre-exists in the rank of The Good, according to all the divine orders.
151.2: For the paternal genus produces the hyparxes of secondary natures, and total powers and essences, through one ineffable transcendency.
151.3: Hence likewise it is denominated paternal, by reason of exhibiting the united and boniform power of The One, and the cause which constitutes secondary natures.
151.4: And in each order of the Gods the paternal genus ranks as the leader, producing all things from itself, and adorning them, because it is arranged analogous to The Good.

152.1: Every thing which is generative in the Gods proceeds according to the infinity of divine power, multiplying itself, proceeding through all things, and transcendently exhibiting a never-failing power in the progressions of secondary natures.
152.2: For to multiply things which proceed, and to produce things into progeny from the occult comprehension in causes, of what else is it the prerogative than of the infinite power of the Gods, through which all divine natures are filled with prolific good? For every thing which is full produces other things from itself through a super-plenary power.

153.1: Every thing perfect in the Gods is the cause of divine perfection.
153.2: For as the hypostases of beings are of one kind, but those of superessential natures of another, so likewise of perfections — those of the Gods themselves are in their hyparxis, but those of beings are secondary and posterior to them.
153.3: And the former are self-perfect and primary, because The Good subsists primarily in them; but the latter possess perfection through participation.

154.1: Every thing which is of a guardian nature in the Gods preserves every thing in its proper order, and is uniformly exempt from secondary and established in primary natures.
154.2: For if a guard immutably preserves the measure of the order of every thing, and connectedly contains all the natures which are guarded in their appropriate perfection, it will impart to all things an excellence superior to subordinate beings, and will firmly establish each thing unmingled in itself, existing as the cause of undefiled purity to the natures which are guarded, and fixing them in superior beings.

155.1: Every thing vivific in the Gods is a generative cause, but every generative cause is not vivific.
155.2: For a generative is more universal than a vivific cause, and is nearer to the principle of all things.
155.3: For generation manifests a cause which produces beings into multitude: but vivification represents to us the deity who is the supplier of all life.
155.4: If therefore the former multiplies the hypostases of beings, but the latter the progressions of life, as being is to life so is the generative order to the vivific causal chain.

156.1: Every cause of purity is contained in the guardian order: but on the contrary every genus of a guardian order is not the same with the purifying genus.
156.2: For purity imparts to all the Gods the unmingled with things inferior, and the undefiled in the providence of secondary natures.
156.3: But a guardian power likewise effects this, contains all things in itself, and firmly inserts them in superior natures.
156.4: The guardian therefore is more universal than the purifying genus.

157.1: Every paternal cause is the supplier of being to all things, and constitutes the hyparxes of beings.
157.2: But every nature which is fabricative of the production of form exists prior to composite natures, and precedes their order and division according to number, and is likewise of the same co-ordination with the paternal cause in the more partial genera of things.
157.3: For each of these is of the order of bound; since hyparxis, number and form have all of them the form of bound: so that in this respect they are co-ordinate with each other.

158.1: Every elevating cause in the Gods differs both from a purifying cause and from the revertive genera.
158.2: For it is evident that this cause has necessarily a primary subsistence in the Gods; since in these all the causes of total good pre-exist.
158.3: But it subsists prior to the purifying cause: for the one liberates from things of a subordinate nature, but the other conjoins with more excellent natures.
158.4: The elevating however has a more partial order than the revertive cause, because every nature which returns, returns either to itself, or to that which is more excellent than itself.

159.1: Every order of the Gods consists of the first principles, Bound, and Infinity; but one order is caused more by Bound, and another by Infinity.
159.2: For every order proceeds from each of these principles, because the impartances of first causes extend through all secondary natures.
159.3: But in some things bound predominates in the mixture of bound and infinity, and in others infinity.
159.4: And thus the genus which has the form of bound is perfected in which the powers of bound dominate: and so too the genus which has the form of the infinite is perfected in which the powers of infinity dominate.

160.1: Every divine intellect is uniform, and perfect; and the first intellect is from itself, and produces other intellects.
160.2: For if it is a God it is filled with divine unities, and is uniform.
160.3: But if this be so, it is likewise perfect, because it is full of divine goodness.
160.4: And if this be admitted, it is likewise primarily intellect, since it is united to the Gods: for deified intellect is better than every intellect.
160.5: But since it is primarily intellect, it likewise imparts an hypostasis to other intellects.
160.6: For all secondary natures receive their hyparxis from the primary natures.

161.1: Every thing which is truly being, and because it depends on the Gods, is divine and imparticipable.
161.2: For since that which is truly being is the first of the natures which participate of the divine union, as has been demonstrated, it likewise fills intellect from itself.
161.3: For intellect is being, because it is filled with being, and true being is therefore a divine intelligible: as that which is deified it is divine, but as that which fills intellect, and is participated by it, it is intelligible.

162.1: Every multitude of unities which illuminates truly existing being is arcane and intelligible; arcane since it is conjoined with The One, but intelligible because it is participated by being.
162.2: For all the Gods are denominated from the things which depend on them; because from these it is possible to know their different hypostases, which are of themselves unknown.
162.3: For every thing divine is of itself ineffable and unknown, because it is connascent with the Ineffable One.

163.1: Every multitude of unities which is participated by imparticipable intellect is intellectual.
163.2: For as intellect is to truly existing being, so are these unities to the intelligible unities.
163.3: If, therefore, the latter which illuminate being are intelligible, hence the former which illuminate a divine and imparticipable intellect are intellectual.
163.4: Yet they are not intellectual in such a way as if they subsisted in intellect, but as causally existing prior to intellect, and generating intellect.

164.1: Every multitude of unities which is participated by every imparticipable soul is supermundane.
164.2: For because imparticipable soul is primarily above the world, the Gods also which are participated by it are likewise supermundane, having the same analogy or proportion to the intellectual and intelligible Gods which soul has to intellect, and intellect to truly existing being.

165.1: Every multitude of unities which is participated by a certain sensible body is mundane.
165.2: For it illuminates the parts of the world through the medium or intervening of intellect and soul.
165.3: For neither is intellect present to any mundane body without soul, nor are deity and soul conjoined immediately, because participations and conjunctions become through similars.
165.4: Hence each of these visible bodies is animated, and moved of itself, through soul: and it possesses a perpetual sameness of subsistence through intellect: but it is divine through union.

166.1: Every intellect is either imparticipable or participable; and if participable, it is either participated by supermundane or by mundane souls.
166.2: For imparticipable intellect, having a primary hyparxis, is the leader of every multitude of intellects.
166.3: But of participable intellects some illuminate the supermundane and imparticipable soul, but others the mundane soul.
166.4: For the mundane multitude does not immediately emanate from the imparticipable, if progressions become through similars.

167.1: Every intellect thinks itself: but the Primal Intellect thinks itself only, and in this intellect Thought and the object of thought are one numerically; but each of the subsequent intellects thinks itself and the natures prior to itself.
167.2: For every intellect either thinks itself, or that which is above itself, or that which is posterior to itself.
167.3: But if it thinks that which is posterior to itself, since it is intellect, it will turn to that which is less excellent than itself.
167.4: And if it thinks that which is above itself, if this is done through the knowledge of itself, it will at one and the same time know itself and that superior nature.
167.5: Hence by knowing the things of which the nature which is superior to it is the cause, it will likewise know itself.

168.1: Every intellect in activity knows that it thinks, and it is not the peculiarity of one intellect to think, and of another to know that it thinks.
168.2: For if it is intellect in activity, and thinks itself to be no other than the object of thought, it will know itself, and see itself.
168.3: But seeing that which thinks, and knowing that which sees, it will know that it is intellect in activity.
168.4: But knowing this, it will know that it thinks, and will not alone know the objects of its thinking.
168.5: Hence it will simultaneously know the intelligible and that it thinks it.

169.1: Every intellect has its essence, power and action in eternity.
169.2: For if intellect thinks itself, and intellect and the intelligible are the same, thought likewise is the same as intellect and the intelligible.
169.3: But that the essence of intellect is eternal is evident — for the whole of it subsists at once — and thinking is likewise eternal, since it is the same with the essence of intellect.
169.4: For if intellect is immovable, it will not be measured by time, neither according to its being nor its activity: but since these subsist with invariable sameness, the power likewise of intellect will be eternal.

170.1: Every intellect thinks all things together; but imparticipable intellect thinks all things together simply: and each of the intellects subsequent to it thinks all things according to one or under the form of the singular.
170.2: For if every intellect establishes its essence in eternity, and together with its essence its activity, it will think all things together.
170.3: For every thing which is successive is in time; the successive consisting of prior and posterior.
170.4: If therefore all intellects similarly think all things, they will not differ from each other.
170.5: Hence each intellect thinks all things according to one.
170.6: For in all intellects there is always the thought of all things, which bounds all things in one of all.

171.1: Every intellect is an impartible essence.
171.2: For if it is without magnitude, incorporeal and immovable, it is impartible.
171.3: For every thing which in any way whatsoever is partible, is either partible by reason of magnitude, or multitude, or of activities which function in time.
171.4: But intellect is eternal in all things, and is beyond bodies, and the multitude which is in it is united.

172.1: Every intellect is proximately the producing cause of natures perpetual and immutable in essence.
172.2: For every nature which is produced by an immovable cause, is immutable in essence.
172.3: But immovable intellect being all things eternally, and abiding in eternity, produces by its very being that which it produces.
172.4: If therefore intellect always is, and is invariably the same, it always produces, and in the same manner.
172.5: Hence it is not the cause of things which at one time exist and at another time not, but it is the cause of things which always exist.

173.1: Every intellect is intellectual, and the things which are prior and posterior to itself are likewise intellectual.
173.2: For the things which are posterior to itself are intellectual through cause, but the things which are prior to itself through participation: but intellect is the same, and is allotted an intellectual essence.
173.3: Hence it defines all things according to its essence; both the things which are through cause, and those which are through participation.

174.1: Every intellect constitutes the things posterior to itself by thinking, and its creation is in thinking, and its thought in creating.
174.2: For if intelligible and intellect are the same, the essence likewise of every intellect will be the same with the thinking in itself.
174.3: But intellect does that which it does through its essence, and produces according to the very being which it is, and by thought therefore it will produce the things which are produced.
174.4: For in intellect being and thought are one.
174.5: If therefore it makes by its very being, but its very being is thought, it makes by thinking.

175.1: Every intellect is primarily participated by those natures which are intellectual both in essence and in activity.
175.2: For it is necessary that every intellect should either be participated by those, or by other natures which have indeed an intellectual essence but do not always think.
175.3: It is however impossible that it should be participated by the latter.
175.4: For the activity of intellect is immovable.
175.5: And hence the natures by which it is participated always participate of intellectual activity, which always causes the participants of it to become intellectual.

176.1: All intellectual forms are in each other, and each is at the same time per se and distinct from the others.
176.2: For if every intellect is impartible, and the multitude which is in it is united through intellectual impartibility, all things in it will be in one, impartibles will be united to each other, and all intellectual forms will pervade through all.
176.3: But if all intellectual forms are immaterial and incorporeal they are unconfused with each other and separate, and each preserving its own purity remains that which it is.
176.4: The peculiar participation however of each participating in a separate manner manifests the unconfused nature of intellectual forms.

177.1: Every intellect being a plenitude of forms, one intellect contains more universal but another more partial forms; and the superior intellects contain more universally the things which those posterior to them contain more partially.
177.2: For the superior intellects use greater powers, because they are more unical than secondary intellects.
177.3: But the inferior intellects, since they are more multiplied, diminish the powers which they contain.
177.4: For things which are more cognate to The One, because they are contracted in quantity are superior in power to the natures which are posterior to them.

178.1: Every intellectual form constitutes eternal natures.
178.2: For if every intellectual form is eternal and immovable, it is essentially the cause of immutable and eternal hypostases, but not of those which become and are corruptible.
178.3: For if all forms produce things posterior to themselves by their very being, but their being has an invariable sameness of subsistence, the things produced by them will likewise be invariably the same, and will be eternal.

179.2: For if there is another multitude posterior to this, essentially inferior to it, and thus more remote from The One, but the intellectual number is nearer to The One, and if that which is nearer to The One is quantitatively less, but that which is more remote from it is quantitatively more, the intellectual number likewise will be less than every multitude posterior to it.
179.4: The multitude of intellects therefore is finite.

180.1: Every intellect is a whole, because each consists of parts, and is at once united to other intellects and differentiated from them; but imparticipable intellect is a whole simply, since it has in itself all the parts totally or under the form of the whole.
180.2: But each partial intellect contains the whole as in a part, and thus is all things partially.
180.3: For if a partial intellect is all things according to one, and a subsistence according to one is nothing else than a subsistence partially, the whole is in each of these intellects partially, being defined according to a certain one particular thing which dominates in all of them.

181.1: Every participated intellect is either divine because it depends on the Gods, or is intellectual only.
181.2: For if there is a divine and imparticipable intellect primarily, the intellect which is cognate to this is not that which differs from it in both respects.
181.3: It is evident therefore that the medium between these is partly similar to that which is primarily intellect, and partly dissimilar to it.
181.4: Either, therefore, it is imparticipable and not divine; or it is participated and divine.
181.5: But every nature imparticipable is divine, because it is allotted an order in multitude analogous to The One.
181.6: Hence there will be a certain Intellect which is divine and at the same time participated.

182.1: Every divine participated intellect is participated by divine souls.
182.2: For if participation assimilates the participant to that which is participated, and renders the former connascent with the latter, it is evident that the participant of a divine intellect must be a divine soul, and dependent on a divine intellect, and that through intellect as a medium it must participate of the deity which it contains.

183.1: Every intellect which is participated indeed, but is intellectual alone, is participated neither by divine souls nor by those which experience a mutation from intellect into a privation of intellect.
183.2: For neither are divine souls of this kind, nor those which participate of intellect.
183.3: For souls participate of the Gods through intellect, as has been demonstrated.
183.4: Nor are souls which admit of mutation of this kind.
183.5: For every intellect is participated by natures which are always intellectual, both in essence and in activity.

184.1: Every soul is either divine, or is that which changes from intellect into a privation of intellect, or that which always remains as a medium between these, but is inferior to divine souls.
184.2: For if divine intellect indeed is participated by divine souls, but that intellect which is intellectual alone by those souls which are neither divine, nor receive a mutation from intelligence into a privation of intellect — for there are souls of this kind which at one time think and at another do not — if this be the case, it is evident that there are three genera of souls.

185.1: All divine souls are Gods psychically; but all those which participate of an intellectual intellect are the perpetual attendants of the Gods; and all those which are the recipients of mutation are only occasionally the attendants of the Gods.
185.2: For if upon some souls the divine light supernally shines, but others always think, and others again only occasionally participate of this perfection, the first of these among the multitude of souls will be analogous to the Gods: and the second will always follow the Gods, by reason of always energizing according to intellect.
185.3: And the souls which only occasionally energize intellectually, can in no way whatsoever be always conjoined with the Gods.

186.1: Every soul is an incorporeal essence and separable from the body.
186.2: For if it knows itself, but every thing which knows itself returns to itself, and that which returns to itself is neither body nor inseparable from body — hence every soul is neither a corporeal essence, nor inseparable from body.
186.3: But that the soul knows itself is evident.
186.4: For if it knows the natures which are above itself, and is naturally able to know itself, much more will it know itself through the causes prior to itself.

187.1: Every soul is indestructible and incorruptible.
187.2: For every thing which can in any way whatsoever be dissolved and destroyed is either corporeal and composite, or is allotted its hypostasis in a subject.
187.3: And that indeed which is dissolved is corrupted because it consists of a multitude of divisible parts: and that of which it is the nature to exist in another vanishes into non-entity when separated from its subject.
187.4: But the soul is incorporeal and external to every subject, subsisting in itself, and returning to itself.
187.5: Hence it is indestructible and incorruptible.

188.1: Every soul is both life and vital.
188.2: For that to which soul accedes necessarily lives, and that which is deprived of soul at once becomes destitute of life.
188.3: If therefore that which is participated introduces life to animated natures it is either life, or vital alone, or both life and vital.
188.4: If however soul is alone vital, but not likewise life, it will consist of life and non-life.
188.5: But if soul is life alone it will no longer participate of the intellectual life.
188.6: Soul however is not imparticipable life.
188.7: And hence it is at the same time both life and vital.

189.2: For if it is able to return to itself, but every thing which returns to itself is self-subsistent, the soul therefore is self-subsistent, and constitutes itself.
189.3: But it is likewise life and vital, and its hyparxis is in vitality.
189.4: And if the participant is fit for participation it immediately becomes animated and vital; soul in effecting this not reasoning nor acting from deliberate choice, but by its very essence imparting life to the participant.
189.5: Hence the being of soul is the same as to live.
189.6: If therefore the soul possesses being from itself and this is the same as to live, soul will be self-vital.

190.1: Every soul is a medium between impartible natures and the natures which are divisible about bodies.
190.2: For if soul is self-vital and self-subsistent, and has an hyparxis separable from bodies, it is exempt from and more excellent than all the natures which are divisible about body: for the corporeal natures are entirely inseparable from their subjects.
190.3: Hence soul is inferior to impartible natures, because it is filled with life externally: but it has been demonstrated that neither does it rank among the natures which are divisible about bodies.
190.4: Hence it is a medium between the two.

191.1: Every participable soul has an eternal essence, but its action is temporal.
191.2: For either it possesses each eternally, or each temporally; or the one eternally, but the other temporally.
191.3: It cannot however possess each eternally: for it would be an impartible essence, and the nature of soul would in no respect differ from an intellectual hypostasis.
191.4: Nor can it possess each temporally: for thus it would be generated only, and would neither be self-vital, nor self-subsistent.
191.5: It follows therefore that every soul is partly eternal, and partly participates of time.
191.6: Hence every participable soul is allotted an eternal essence, but a temporal action.

192.1: Every participable soul ranks among the number of truly existing beings, and is the first of generated natures.
192.2: For if it is essentially eternal it is truly being through its hyparxis, and always is.
192.3: For that which participates of eternity participates likewise of perpetual existence.
192.4: But if it is in time according to action, it is generated.
192.5: For every thing which participates of time, since it is always becoming to be according to the prior and posterior of time, is wholly generated.
192.6: But if every soul is in a certain respect generated through its action, it will be the first of generated natures.

193.1: Every soul subsists proximately from intellect.
193.2: For if it has an immutable and eternal essence, it proceeds from an immovable essence.
193.3: For that which proceeds from a movable cause, is essentially changed in every respect.
193.4: The cause therefore of every soul is immovable.
193.5: But if it proximately subsists from intellect, it is perfected by and returns to intellect.
193.6: And if it participates of the knowledge which intellect imparts to the natures which are able to partake of it, every soul proceeds from intellect.

194.1: Every soul contains all the forms which intellect primarily possesses.
194.2: For if soul proceeds from intellect, and intellect constitutes it; and if intellect subsisting immovably produces all things by its very being, it will likewise impart to soul which it constitutes the essential reasons or productive principles of all things which it contains.
194.3: For every thing which produces by its very being imparts secondarily to the thing generated by it that which it is itself primarily.
194.4: The soul therefore contains secondarily the representations of intellectual forms.

195.1: Every soul is all things, containing sensibles paradigmatically, but intelligibles iconically.
195.2: For subsisting as a medium between impartible natures and those which are divisible about body, it produces and constitutes the latter of these, but pre-establishes in itself the causes from which it proceeds.
195.3: Those things, therefore, of which it is the pre-existent cause it antecedently comprehends paradigmatically or in their pre-formed models.
195.4: But it has by participation the causes of its subsistence.
195.5: Hence the soul is all beings, containing those which are primary by participation, but paradigmatically those which are posterior to its own nature.

196.1: Every participable soul primarily uses a perpetual body, which has an unbegotten and incorruptible hypostasis.
196.2: For if every soul is essentially eternal, and by its very being primarily animates some particular body, it will always animate this body: for the essence of soul is immutable.
196.3: But if this be the case, that which is animated by it is always animated, and always participates of the life of soul: and that which always lives by a much greater priority always exists.
196.4: But that which always is, is perpetual.
196.5: Hence that which is primarily attached to every soul is perpetual.

197.1: Every soul is an essence vital and gnostic, and a life essential and gnostic, and is knowledge, essence, and life; all these, the essential, the vital, and the gnostic, subsist in it together; and all are in all, and each is apart from the others.
197.2: For if it is the medium between impartible forms and those which are divided about bodies, since in intellectual natures all things subsist in union, they are distinguished and divided in souls.
197.3: All things, therefore, subsist together and at the same time apart in these.
197.4: But if all impartibles subsist together and in one they pervade through each other, and if they are separate they are again divided without confusion; so that each subsists by itself, and all are in all.

198.1: Every nature which participates of time, and is always moved, is measured by circuits.
198.2: For since it is measured by time, the motion of it likewise participates of the measure and bound of time, and proceeds according to number: but because it is always moved, and this always is not eternal but temporal, it is necessary that it should use circuits.
198.3: For motion is a mutation from some things to others.
198.4: These however being finite, there can neither be a mutation to infinity according to a right line, nor can that which is always moved make its transitions finitely.
198.5: Hence that which is always moved will proceed from the same to the same.

199.1: Every mundane soul uses circuits of its proper life, and restitutions to its pristine state.
199.2: For if it is measured by time, it acts transitively and has a peculiar motion.
199.3: But every nature which is moved and participates of time, if it is perpetual uses circuits, periodically revolves, and proceeding from the same to the same is restored to its former state.
199.4: And every mundane soul having motion, and energizing in time, will have circuits of motions, and restitutions to its pristine state.

200.1: Every circuit of soul is measured by time; the circuit of other souls is measured by a certain time, but the circuit of the first soul measured by time is measured by the whole of time.
200.2: For if all motions have prior and posterior, so likewise have circuits, and on this account they participate of time.
200.3: That the soul, therefore, which is primarily measured by time is measured by the whole of time, is evident.
200.4: For if time is the measure of all motion, that which is primarily moved will participate of all time, and will be measured by the whole of time.

201.1: All divine souls have triple energies: one as souls, another as receiving a divine intellect, and another as attached to the Gods; and they provide for the whole of things as Gods, but know all things through an intellectual life, and move bodies through a self-motive essence.
201.2: For because they psychically participate of the natures which are superior to them, and are not simply souls but divine souls, and have an order in the psychical extent analogous to the Gods, they energize not only psychically but likewise divinely, being allotted a divine summit of their essence, and because they likewise have an intellectual hypostasis, through which they are placed under intellectual essences.

202.1: All souls attending upon and always following the Gods are inferior to divine, but are developed above partial souls.
202.2: For divine souls participate of intellect and deity, and hence are at the same time intellectual and divine, and the leaders of other souls, just as the Gods likewise are the leaders of all beings.
202.3: But partial souls are deprived of an attachment to intellect, because they are not able to participate proximately of an intellectual essence.
202.4: Hence the souls which always follow the Gods are of a mediate condition: for though they receive a perfect intellect, and through this surpass partial souls, yet they are not attached to the divine unities.

203.1: Of every psychical multitude, divine souls are greater in power than other souls, but less in number; but those which always follow divine souls have a mediate order among all souls, both in power and quantity; and partial souls are inferior in power to the others, but proceed into a greater number.
203.2: For divine souls are more allied to The One, on account of a divine hyparxis, but souls of a mediate rank through the participation of intellect.
203.3: Among perpetual natures, those which are nearer to The One are more single in number, but those which are more remote from The One are more multiplied.

204.1: Every divine soul is a leader of many souls which always follow the Gods, and of a still greater number of those which occasionally receive this order.
204.2: For since it is divine it is necessary that it should be allotted an order which is the leader of all things, and which has a primary rank among souls.
204.3: For in all beings that which is divine is the leader of wholes.
204.4: It is likewise requisite that every divine soul should preside over the souls which perpetually follow the Gods, and through these as media, preside over the partial souls.
204.5: For every soul likewise of those which always follow the Gods is the leader of a multitude of partial souls, imitating in this a divine soul.

205.1: Every partial soul has the same ratio to the soul under which it is essentially arranged, as the vehicle of the one has to the vehicle of the other.
205.2: For if the distribution of vehicles to all souls is according to nature, it is necessary that the vehicle of every partial soul should have the same ratio to the vehicle of the soul which ranks as a whole, as the essence of the one has to the essence of the other.
205.3: The distribution, however, is according to nature.
205.4: For the things which primarily participate are spontaneously conjoined with the natures which they participate.

206.1: Every partial soul is able to descend infinitely into generation, and to reascend from generation to real being.
206.2: For if it at one time follows the Gods, but at another falls from the striving upwards to the divine nature, it is evident that it is alternatively conversant with generation and the Gods.
206.3: Since it is not for an infinite time with the Gods, it will not for the whole of the succeeding time be conversant with bodies.
206.4: For that which has no temporal beginning will never have an end, and that which has no end is necessarily without a beginning.
206.5: It follows, therefore, that every partial soul makes circuits of ascents from and of descents into generation, and that this must be unceasing through infinite time.

207.1: The vehicle of every partial soul is fabricated by an immovable cause.
207.2: For if it is perpetually and connascently attached to the soul which uses it, and by cognation is immutable in essence, it is allotted its hypostasis from an immovable cause.
207.3: For every thing which is generated from movable causes is essentially changed.
207.4: Moreover, every soul has a perpetual body, which primarily participates of it.
207.5: Hence the cause of a partial soul, and therefore of its vehicle, is immovable, and on this account supermundane.

208.1: The vehicle of every partial soul is immaterial, essentially indivisible, and impassive.
208.2: For if it proceeds from an immovable fabrication, and is perpetual, it will have an immaterial and impassive hypostasis.
208.3: For the things which are naturally passive in essence are all mutable and material, and because they subsist differently at different times are attached to movable causes.
208.4: But that the vehicle of every partial soul is indivisible, is manifest.
208.5: For every thing which is divided, so far as it is divided is corrupted, because it departs from the whole, and from its continuity.

209.1: The vehicle of every partial soul descends indeed with the addition of more material vestments, but becomes united to the soul by an ablation of every thing material, and a recurrence to its proper form, analogous to the soul which uses it.
209.2: For the soul indeed descends irrationally, assuming irrational lives; but it ascends, laying aside all the generation-producing powers, with which it was invested in its descent, and becoming pure returns to the pristine condition of its nature.
209.3: For the vehicle imitates the lives of the souls which use it, and since they are every where moved it is moved in conjunction with them.

210.1: Every connascent vehicle of the soul always has the same figure and magnitude; but it appears to be greater and less and of a dissimilar figure through the additions and ablations of other bodies.
210.2: For if it derives its essence from an immovable cause, it is evident that both its figure and its magnitude are defined by this cause, and each is immutable and invariable.
210.3: But at different times it appears to be different, as likewise greater and less.
210.4: Hence through other bodies, added from the material elements, and again taken away, it exhibits a different appearance both in quantity and form.

211.1: Every partial soul descending into generation descends as a whole; nor does one part of it remain on high, and another part descend.
211.2: For if part of the soul remains in the Intelligible World it will always think, either without transition, or by a transitive process.
211.3: But if without transition it will be pure intellect and not a part of the soul, and the partial soul will directly participate of intellect.
211.5: But if it thinks by a transitive process, then out of that which always thinks and that which occasionally thinks one essence will be formed.
211.7: For these always differ, as has been demonstrated.
211.8: Every partial soul, therefore, descends as a whole.
